tests.label: terms related to food and culinary subjects
should_fire: She stirred the tomato sauce and added fresh basil.
The recipe calls for two cups of flour and a pinch of salt.
near_miss: She stirred the paint and added a second coat to the wall.
He filed the report and added his signature at the bottom.
tests.basis: Concrete topic; plain on-topic sentences should fire if the label holds.

tests.label: references to the Windows operating system
should_fire: Windows 11 keeps asking me to restart for updates.
He reinstalled Windows after the laptop crashed.
near_miss: She opened the windows to let in some fresh air.
Linux keeps asking me to restart for updates.
tests.basis: Named product in plain sentences; near-misses swap the sense or the OS.

tests.label: geographical and administrative terms related to specific regions or districts
should_fire: The province announced new funding for rural roads.
Voters in the county will decide the measure in November.
near_miss: She announced new funding for the community garden.
The committee published its annual report on Friday.
tests.basis: Common administrative words; risk is breadth, but plain reading says pass.

tests.label: references to ancient figures and mythological or legendary elements
should_fire: Zeus hurled thunderbolts from Mount Olympus.
The legend says King Arthur pulled the sword from the stone.
near_miss: The president addressed the nation from the capital.
She read a novel about a detective in modern London.
tests.basis: Concrete mythological content in both should-fires.

tests.label: shipping-related terms and phrases for large items
should_fire: The freight company will deliver the piano on a pallet.
They shipped the industrial press by container and insured the cargo.
near_miss: She mailed the letter in a standard envelope.
They delivered the speech to a packed auditorium.
tests.basis: Large-item shipping terms in plain sentences; near-misses shrink or metaphorize.

tests.label: moments of surprise or unexpected events, particularly those that are positive or celebratory in nature.
should_fire: He had no idea about the party, and he gasped when everyone shouted surprise.
Out of nowhere, she won the raffle and laughed in disbelief.
near_miss: They threw her a birthday party she had helped plan for weeks.
He was shocked and upset when the pipe burst flooded the kitchen.
tests.basis: Label bundles surprise with positive celebration; the two senses likely split.

tests.label: references to light and illumination contexts
should_fire: The lamp filled the room with warm light.
Sunlight streamed through the window all morning.
near_miss: The suitcase was light enough to carry with one hand.
She packed a light jacket for the trip.
tests.basis: Polysemous label word; the weight sense likely fires as well.

tests.label: references to the name “Tom”
should_fire: Tom called to say he would be late.
I asked Tom to review the draft.
near_miss: John called to say he would be late.
She sliced the tomatoes for the salad.
tests.basis: A specific name; swap and string probes are the honest near-misses.

tests.label: periods and punctuation that signify the end of sentences
should_fire: The meeting ended early. Everyone went home.
She finished the letter. Then she sealed the envelope.
near_miss: The meeting ended early, and everyone went home
Did the meeting end early? She certainly hoped so!
tests.basis: Terminal punctuation is everywhere, including inside the near-misses; isolating it in lone sentences is doubtful.

tests.label: references to literary works and notable authors
should_fire: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet and Macbeth.
We studied Dickens in my English literature class.
near_miss: The plumber fixed the sink and replaced a valve.
She wrote an email to her manager about the schedule.
tests.basis: Named authors and works in plain sentences.

tests.label: specific scientific or technical terms related to genetics and molecular biology
should_fire: The BRCA1 gene mutation raises the risk of breast cancer.
Scientists sequenced the DNA to find the mutation.
near_miss: The telescope revealed a new comet near Jupiter.
The doctor said the condition can run in families.
tests.basis: Technical genetics terms in plain sentences; one near-miss is heredity without the vocabulary.

tests.label: concepts related to reputation and its effects
should_fire: The scandal ruined the senator's reputation.
She built a reputation as an honest broker over twenty years.
near_miss: The scandal ruined the senator's chances in the primary.
He built a house on the edge of town.
tests.basis: The label's own word in plain sentences; near-misses keep the frame, drop the concept.

tests.label: phrases related to diversity and inclusion in various contexts
should_fire: The company hired a more diverse leadership team this year.
The school's inclusion program pairs new students with mentors.
near_miss: The company hired a more experienced leadership team this year.
The garden has a diverse mix of vegetables this year.
tests.basis: Label terms in their social sense; one-word swap and one sense swap as near-misses.

tests.label: elements of personal relationships and family connections
should_fire: She called her mother every Sunday morning.
His brother and sister flew in for Thanksgiving.
near_miss: She called her accountant every Sunday morning.
The company is a family of brands under one parent firm.
tests.basis: Family members in plain sentences; person swap and metaphor as near-misses.

tests.label: details about concert schedules and ticket sales
should_fire: Tickets for the concert go on sale Friday at noon.
The band added a second show in Chicago after the first sold out.
near_miss: Tickets for the train to Chicago go on sale Friday at noon.
The band practiced in the garage all afternoon.
tests.basis: Concert sales and scheduling language; event swap and no-sales near-misses.

tests.label: expressions of “coolness” or related positive attributes
should_fire: He stayed cool under pressure during the final round.
That jacket looks really cool on you.
near_miss: The soup had cooled by the time we sat down.
She stayed calm under pressure during the final round.
tests.basis: Label bundles composure, style, and temperature; the senses likely split.

tests.label: concepts related to simplicity and straightforwardness
should_fire: The instructions are simple enough for a child to follow.
It's a straightforward fix that takes five minutes.
near_miss: The instructions are detailed enough to fill a whole binder.
The recipe has a simple list of ingredients but a complicated method.
tests.basis: Label's own words in plain sentences; opposite and mixed near-misses.

tests.label: terms related to medical conditions and anatomical processes
should_fire: The infection spread to her lungs within days.
His broken ankle needed surgery and six weeks in a cast.
near_miss: The rumor spread to every office within days.
The broken pipe needed repair and six weeks of roadwork.
tests.basis: Medical events in plain sentences; structure-matched swaps as near-misses.

tests.label: elements related to buttons in a UI or web interface
should_fire: Click the blue submit button at the bottom of the form.
The button turns gray when the option is unavailable.
near_miss: She sewed a button back onto his coat.
Click the blue link at the bottom of the form.
tests.basis: UI sense in plain sentences; clothing sense and link swap as near-misses.

tests.label: references to a specific shoe brand
should_fire: He bought a new pair of Nike running shoes.
Her Adidas sneakers were worn out after a year.
near_miss: He bought a new pair of running shoes.
Her sneakers were worn out after a year of training.
tests.basis: The label never names the brand, so a plain test cannot target it; generic brands may miss the specific one.

tests.label: references to personal beliefs, self-identification, and emotional experiences
should_fire: She identifies as an independent voter and believes in small government.
He says his faith shapes how he votes.
near_miss: The form asks applicants to identify their employer and address.
He believes the package will arrive on Friday.
tests.basis: Label bundles belief, self-identification, and emotion; likely fragments across them.

tests.label: discussions and references to issues of racism and discriminatory behaviors
should_fire: The report documented racist hiring practices at the company.
He was fired for making racist remarks to a coworker.
near_miss: The report documented careless hiring practices at the company.
The town debated the new zoning rules at the meeting.
tests.basis: The label's own word in plain sentences; one-word swap as near-miss.

tests.label: phrases that indicate summary or overall conclusions
should_fire: In summary, the plan saves money and time.
All in all, the trip went smoothly.
near_miss: The summary of the report is on page two.
She added up the total cost of the trip.
tests.basis: Summary phrases as sentence openers; noun use and literal adding as near-misses.

tests.label: words related to reading devices and the eBook industry
should_fire: She reads novels on her Kindle every night.
The e-reader's battery lasts for weeks.
near_miss: She reads novels in a paperback every night.
He charged his phone and tablet before the flight.
tests.basis: Named device category in plain sentences; format swap and other devices as near-misses.

tests.label: questions and inquiries about various topics or contexts
should_fire: What time does the train leave?
She asked whether the store was still open.
near_miss: The train leaves at six in the morning.
Please find the answer in the attached document.
tests.basis: A question is a form, not a topic; statements about questions blur the line the label draws.

tests.label: expressions of happiness and positive emotions
should_fire: She was thrilled when she heard the good news.
The kids laughed with joy at the surprise.
near_miss: She was relieved when she heard the news.
The kids shouted with anger at the referee.
tests.basis: Positive emotion words in plain sentences; adjacent and opposite emotions as near-misses.

tests.label: references to different types and characteristics of pipes
should_fire: The plumber replaced the copper pipes under the sink.
Water pressure dropped because a pipe burst down the street.
near_miss: He smoked a pipe on the porch every evening.
The organ pipes filled the hall with sound.
tests.basis: The label spans pipe types; if other pipe senses fire too, the near-misses beat the rule.

tests.label: discussions related to music and artistic collaborations
should_fire: The two singers recorded a duet for the new album.
She collaborated with a jazz drummer on the track.
near_miss: The two singers recorded solo albums in the same year.
She practiced the piano alone every morning.
tests.basis: Collaboration language in plain sentences; solo work as near-misses.

tests.label: negative phrases and expressions related to obligation or denial
should_fire: You must not leave the gate unlocked.
He said he would not pay for the repairs.
near_miss: You should leave the gate unlocked tonight.
He said he would gladly pay for the repairs.
tests.basis: Negation and obligation words are concrete; positive counterparts as near-misses.

tests.label: products related to fashion and beauty
should_fire: She bought a new lipstick and a bottle of foundation.
The store sells designer handbags and silk scarves.
near_miss: She bought a new hammer and a box of nails.
The store sells fresh bread and pastries.
tests.basis: Product categories in plain sentences; other product domains as near-misses.

tests.label: forward-looking statements regarding business projections and associated risks
should_fire: The company expects revenue to grow by ten percent next year.
Management warned that future results may fall short of forecasts.
near_miss: The company grew revenue by ten percent last year.
Management described the new office layout in detail.
tests.basis: Forward-looking corporate language; past-tense swap as the key near-miss.

tests.label: terms related to control and regulation
should_fire: New regulations will control how much banks can lend.
The agency regulates food safety across the country.
near_miss: He controlled his temper during the argument.
The remote control stopped working during the movie.
tests.basis: Label spans regulatory and everyday senses of the same word; everyday senses likely fire too.

tests.label: references to crafting materials and methods
should_fire: She glued the felt pieces onto the cardboard base.
He carved the block of wood with a small knife.
near_miss: She assembled the metal engine parts on the workbench.
She bought the finished quilt at the craft fair.
tests.basis: Hand-crafting materials and actions; industrial assembly and buying-finished as near-misses.

tests.label: terms related to electricity and power infrastructure
should_fire: The storm knocked out power to three thousand homes.
Crews repaired the transmission lines by morning.
near_miss: The mayor holds a lot of power in this town.
She raised her voice to be heard over the crowd.
tests.basis: Grid and outage language; political sense of the same word as near-miss.

tests.label: terms related to governance and political processes
should_fire: The city council voted to approve the new budget.
Parliament debated the bill for three days.
near_miss: The book club voted to pick next month's novel.
The company board approved the new budget on Tuesday.
tests.basis: Government process in plain sentences; non-government voting and corporate approval as near-misses.

tests.label: terms related to colors and color coding
should_fire: The red car stopped at the green light.
She wore a blue dress with white shoes.
near_miss: The car stopped at the traffic light on Main Street.
She wore a dress with matching shoes to the party.
tests.basis: Color words in plain sentences; same scenes with colors removed as near-misses.

tests.label: phrases that highlight the concept of “short” in various contexts
should_fire: The meeting was short, only fifteen minutes.
He wrote a short note and left it on the desk.
near_miss: They ran short of coffee before the guests arrived.
She ordered a shortbread cookie with her tea.
tests.basis: Label bundles the word's senses; shortage sense and the letter string likely bleed across.

tests.label: mentions of the term “Mercury,” particularly in relation to its propulsion systems and legal implications
should_fire: Mercury is the closest planet to the sun.
The thermometer broke and spilled mercury on the lab floor.
near_miss: Venus is the second planet from the sun.
The lab measured the temperature with a digital sensor.
tests.basis: Label bundles unrelated senses of one word, plus propulsion and legal senses; a single feature is unlikely to cover the bundle.

tests.label: references to the color yellow and its variations
should_fire: The yellow school bus stopped at the corner.
She painted the kitchen a soft yellow.
near_miss: The red school bus stopped at the corner.
The pages of the old book had yellowed over time.
tests.basis: One specific color; color swap and verb form as near-misses.

tests.label: questions and statements regarding intentions, plans, or purposes
should_fire: She intends to apply for the job next week.
We plan to repaint the kitchen this spring.
near_miss: She applied for the job last week.
The hammer's purpose is driving nails.
tests.basis: Stated intentions and plans; completed action and object purpose as near-misses.
